subject: afm
title: Mutual Funds
summary: NAV · returns and effective yield · dividend equalisation · plan-wise yield · Sharpe/Treynor → NAV
currency: SM Nov 2024 ed. (reprint Aug 2025), applicable for May 2026 onwards · no amendments for Nov 2026

cards.front: What is a mutual fund, and how is the return shared?

back.simplified: A trust that pools savings of many investors with a common goal by issuing units, and invests in capital and money market instruments. Net income and capital appreciation are shared in proportion to units held.
back.explanation: The investor is a part owner of all the fund's assets and liabilities. The fund house charges fees based on assets managed.

cards.front: Why might a small investor prefer a mutual fund to buying shares directly?

back.simplified: Diversification needs 15–20 stocks; ₹5,000 can't do that alone but buys a wide basket through a fund. SIPs build discipline. Stock picking needs time, skill and inclination.
back.trap: Choosing shares because their price is under ₹50 or ₹100 — the SM says price should never be the criterion.

cards.front: Name the four constituents needed to establish a mutual fund in India.

back.simplified: Sponsor → Trust (trustees) → Asset Management Company → Custodian, all under SEBI registration.
back.explanation: Sponsor = promoter (initial capital, appoints trustees). Trust deed registered under the Registration Act, 1908. AMC manages schemes. Custodian holds the securities.

cards.front: Sponsor track record, sponsor's share of AMC net worth, AMC net worth, independent directors, AMC removal — the numbers?

back.simplified: Sponsor: 5 years in financial services, at least 40% of AMC net worth. AMC net worth ₹100 crore (SM). Trustees ⅔ independent; AMC 50% independent. AMC removed by majority of trustees or 75% of unit holders.

cards.front: Who holds the securities of a mutual fund, and what must it be independent of?

back.simplified: A SEBI-registered custodian — independent of the sponsor and the AMC. For demat securities, a Depository Participant.

cards.front: Open-ended vs close-ended: how does an investor enter and exit each?

back.simplified: Open-ended: buy and redeem any time with the fund; unlimited capital; no maturity. Close-ended: buy in the NFO or on the exchange after listing; exit by selling on the exchange, at maturity, or in a repurchase window.

cards.front: How do interval funds differ from close-ended funds? (3 points)

back.simplified: 1) Need not be listed — in-built redemption window. 2) Can issue fresh units during the interval at NAV-based prices. 3) No defined maturity.

cards.front: What four risks does a bond fund carry?

back.simplified: I-C-P-R: Interest rate risk, Credit risk, Prepayment risk (callable bonds called when rates fall), Reinvestment risk (maturity proceeds reinvested at lower rates).
back.trap: Reinvestment risk is favourable when rates rise.

cards.front: Growth, aggressive and income equity funds — who is each for?

back.simplified: Growth: long-term capital appreciation, long-term investors. Aggressive: start-ups, IPOs, speculative shares, risk takers. Income: high-dividend safe stocks and high-yield money market, current income seekers.

cards.front: International fund vs offshore fund?

back.simplified: International: raises money in India, invests globally. Offshore: located outside India, raises money globally to invest in India.

cards.front: Where does a capital protection oriented fund get its protection, and what does SEBI require of it?

back.simplified: From its portfolio structure (mostly high-rated debt, some equity) — not a bank guarantee or insurance. Must be close-ended, listed, and its intended portfolio structure rated by a credit rating agency.
back.trap: It is not a capital guaranteed scheme.

cards.front: Quant fund: how does it work, and how is its manager different from an index fund manager?

back.simplified: Rule-based statistical models decide stock, quantity and timing. The index manager just follows the index; the quant manager designs and monitors the models and modifies them.
back.explanation: Pros: no human bias, consistent strategy, lower expense ratio. Con: models rest on historical data.

cards.front: What is a fund of funds?

back.simplified: A scheme that invests in units of other mutual fund schemes, of the same or other fund houses — e.g. Indian MFs investing in international MF schemes.

cards.front: What is a direct plan and why is its NAV higher?

back.simplified: Introduced by SEBI from 1 January 2013. The AMC charges no distribution expenses, trail fees or transaction charges, so expenses are lower and NAV higher than the regular plan.

cards.front: Flexicap vs multicap?

back.simplified: Flexicap: any proportion across market caps. Multicap: at least 25% each in large, mid and small caps; remaining 25% at discretion.

cards.front: Which risk does an FMP avoid, and which does it still carry?

back.simplified: Free from interest rate risk — investments mature with the fund. Still carries credit risk (default or downgrade).
back.explanation: Close-ended, bought in the NFO, listed but thinly traded so illiquid. Many have 3-year tenure for indexation and hold some AA and lower paper for yield.

cards.front: ELSS: tax section, lock-in and why invest via SIP?

back.simplified: s.80C, 3-year lock-in. SIP avoids a year-end lump sum and averages cost.

cards.front: Sector fund vs thematic fund?

back.simplified: Sector: one industry, rides its cycle — risky, only a small part of a portfolio, not for first-timers. Thematic: broader theme (multi-sector, international, commodity), but the market may take long to recognise the theme.

cards.front: What does an arbitrage fund exploit?

back.simplified: Price differences between the spot and futures markets — low-volatility returns better than typical debt, lower volatility than equity.

cards.front: Growth option vs dividend payout vs dividend reinvestment?

back.simplified: Growth: nothing paid out; gain on withdrawal. Payout: dividend paid; NAV falls by it. Reinvestment: dividend reinvested at ex-dividend NAV, giving extra units.

cards.front: What makes an ETF different from an open-ended index fund?

back.simplified: It is listed and trades through the day at real-time prices close to NAV; an open-ended fund deals once a day at NAV. Authorised participants act as market makers.
back.explanation: Low cost, tax efficient, no paperwork. Types: index, commodity, bond, currency ETFs.

cards.front: Three differences between a hedge fund and a mutual fund.

back.simplified: Lightly regulated private vehicle for selected clients; discloses little publicly; charges a performance fee (losses borne by investors). Uses leverage, long/short and derivatives to maximise return.

cards.front: ANP Plan: ₹20 crore, 0.10% fixed + 2% above the ₹21 crore high-water mark. Fee at 29%, 4.5%, −1.8%?

back.trap: Charging the incentive on the year's gain instead of the excess over ₹21 crore.

cards.front: ₹10 lakh for 10 years, 12% gross; regular TER 1.8% vs direct 1.0%. Ending values?
List the 12 advantages of mutual funds.

back.simplified: Professional management, diversification, convenient administration, higher returns, low cost (2.5% cap), liquidity, transparency, other benefits (SIP/SWP/switch), highly regulated, economies of scale, flexibility, convenience.

cards.front: Four drawbacks of mutual funds?

back.simplified: No guarantee of return (underperformance, entry/exit timing, crashes); diversification caps upside; picking the right fund is hard and past performance doesn't predict; costs, and AMC fees are not linked to performance.

cards.front: Which advantage carries a SEBI number in the SM, and what is it?

back.simplified: Low cost of management: maximum 2.50% for equity funds; any extra cost borne by the AMC.

cards.front: Write the NAV formula with every item in net assets.

back.simplified: NAV = net assets ÷ units outstanding. Net assets = market value of investments + receivables + accrued income + other assets − accrued expenses − payables − other liabilities.

cards.front: An investor sends a cheque and the fund buys shares with part of it. How many units, and what happens to NAV?

back.simplified: Units issued = cheque ÷ current (unrounded) NAV. NAV is unchanged that day; the unused money sits as cash. Next day revalue all shares (including the new ones) + cash ÷ new units.
cases: SM TYK: ₹30 lakh ÷ 78.8366 → 6,38,053 units; new NAV ₹82.26

cards.front: How does ICAI value listed shares bought at an old index level, and unlisted bonds with a diminution?

back.simplified: Shares: cost × present index ÷ index at purchase (₹20 cr × 2,300 ÷ 1,000 = ₹46 cr). Unlisted bonds: cost less the diminution (₹1 cr × 80%).
back.trap: "175% of face value" means ₹175 on a ₹100 share — not 175% of the ₹160 cost.

cards.front: Formulae for public offer price and redemption price?

back.simplified: POP = NAV ÷ (1 − front-end load). Redemption = NAV ÷ (1 + back-end load). Alternative: load = price difference ÷ NAV.
back.explanation: Exit load goes back into the scheme, not to the AMC. No scheme charges entry load now.

cards.front: Formula for the return a scheme must earn to match what the investor earns alone?

back.simplified: r₂ = r₁ ÷ (1 − initial expenses) + recurring expenses.

cards.front: What does the expense ratio include and exclude?

back.simplified: Includes management and advisory fees, travel, audit, custodian, registrar, consultancy. Excludes brokerage on portfolio trades. Also called MER or TER.

cards.front: What is trail commission and how is it calculated?

back.simplified: Annual fee to the distributor while money stays invested: 0.30–0.75% of the investment, on daily average AUM, paid monthly. Separate from upfront commission.

cards.front: What is side pocketing and whom does it protect?

back.simplified: Moving downgraded/illiquid (stressed) assets out of the main portfolio so NAV reflects only liquid assets. Protects continuing long-term holders and avoids distress selling.
cases: IL&FS default — funds wrote off exposure, giving low or negative returns

cards.front: Define tracking error, give its formula and four causes.

back.simplified: Deviation of a fund's return from its benchmark. TE = √[Σ(d − d̄)² ÷ (n − 1)]. Causes: transaction cost, AMC fees, fund expenses, cash holdings, sampling bias.
back.trap: Higher TE means higher risk even if the fund outperforms.

cards.front: What is dividend equalisation and how does it change issue and repurchase prices?

back.simplified: A new investor pays (and an exiting investor receives) the undistributed income per unit to date. Issue price = NAV + entry load + income per unit; repurchase = NAV − exit load + income per unit.
cases: SM TYK: issue ₹19.2015, repurchase ₹18.564, NAV 30 June ₹20.2670

cards.front: A gilt fund expects rates to fall 25 bp. What does the manager do to duration, and how?

back.simplified: Lengthen average duration: sell the shortest bond, buy the longest (7.85 → 9.75 years in RTP Nov 2026). If rates are to rise, shorten it (→ 6.55 years).
back.explanation: Longer duration = bigger price rise when rates fall.

cards.front: NAV ₹10, POP ₹10.204, redemption ₹9.80. Front-end and back-end load by ICAI's formula?
Return on a fund that pays income and capital-gain distributions?

back.simplified: r = (NAV₁ − NAV₀ + I + G) ÷ NAV₀. With reinvestment: extra units = distributions ÷ reinvestment NAV; return = (all units × closing NAV − cost) ÷ cost.
cases: SM TYK: payout 23.43% vs reinvest 24.85% → reinvest

cards.front: Effective yield p.a. on a scheme held for some days?

back.simplified: [(units × closing NAV − investment) + dividends] ÷ investment × 365 ÷ days × 100.
back.trap: Using months instead of exact days.

cards.front: You know the effective yield p.a. and the period's actual yield. How do you find the investment date?

back.simplified: Days = period yield % × 365 ÷ effective yield p.a.; count back from the valuation date.

cards.front: A plan declares a 20% dividend. 10,487.80 units, NAV ₹25.95. How many new units on reinvestment?

back.simplified: Dividend = units × ₹10 face value × 20% = ₹20,975.60; new units = 20,975.60 ÷ 25.95 = 808.31.
back.trap: Dividend % is on face value, not on NAV.

cards.front: How do you compare dividend-reinvestment, bonus and growth plans?

back.simplified: Build a units table for each plan to redemption; value = units × closing NAV; deduct STT and STCG on short-term units only; annual return = gain ÷ investment × 12 ÷ months (or IRR).

cards.front: ABC MF April: how is the investor's 12% annual rate of earning built?

back.simplified: Closing NAV ₹9.90 from closing cash ₹0.80 lakh + portfolio ₹198 lakh − arrears ₹0.80 lakh over 20 lakh units. Per unit: distributions ₹0.20 − capital loss ₹0.10 = ₹0.10 on ₹10 = 1% a month = 12% a year.

cards.front: Annual return 16%, opening NAV ₹78.50, distributions ₹0.40 + ₹0.30. Month-end NAV?
How do you find the issue price of a bonus plan from its average yield?

back.simplified: Value now = investment × (1 + yield × years); units now = value ÷ NAV; undo bonuses latest first (× b/(a+b)); issue price = investment ÷ original units.

cards.front: Why can a closed-ended fund investor earn more (or less) than the NAV growth?

back.simplified: He buys and sells at market price = NAV × (1 ± premium/discount). If the discount narrows or a premium appears, his return beats NAV growth.
cases: PYQ May 2026: GM return 3.771% vs NAV growth 2.76%

cards.front: Four steps of a dividend-equalisation sum?

back.simplified: 1) income per unit each month on the units outstanding; 2) add equalisation on issue / deduct on repurchase; 3) dividend = % × available income; 4) closing NAV = all inflows − outflows ÷ closing units.

cards.front: Effective yields known; find the initial investment (Mr S, PYQ Nov 2023).

back.simplified: Period yield = yield p.a. × days ÷ 365; total ₹ yield = dividend + NAV change; investment = ₹ yield ÷ period yield → ₹10 lakh, ₹10 lakh, ₹5 lakh.

cards.front: In a "new fund, one month" NAV sum, which three items do students get wrong?

back.simplified: 1) Only expenses paid leave cash; arrears are deducted from net assets. 2) Distribute % of realised earnings only (sale gain + dividend). 3) Uncollected dividend is a receivable; an underwriter taking up the whole issue means all units are outstanding.

cards.front: Name the five quantitative parameters for evaluating a fund.

back.simplified: Risk-adjusted returns; benchmark returns (alpha); comparison with peers; returns across economic and market cycles; financial measures — expense ratio, Sharpe, Treynor, Sortino.

cards.front: Sharpe vs Treynor vs Sortino: which risk is in the denominator?

back.simplified: Sharpe: total risk σ. Treynor: systematic risk β (against the fund's benchmark). Sortino: downside deviation.

cards.front: Three qualitative parameters for evaluating a fund?

back.simplified: Quality of portfolio (blue chips, diversification, style; for debt credit quality, maturity, modified duration; low turnover); track record and competence of the fund manager; credibility of the fund house team.

cards.front: Sharpe 2, σ 11.25, Treynor 15, NAV ₹70.71 with 99% equity, market falls 5%, costs ₹3 a year. Expected NAV after a month?

back.trap: Applying β to the cash part too.

cards.front: Given correlation, σ of the fund and the market variance, how do you get β and then Treynor?

back.simplified: σ_m = √variance; β = ρ × σ_p ÷ σ_m; Treynor = (R_p − R_f) ÷ β.

cards.front: From Sharpe and Treynor, how do you reach the coefficient of determination?

back.simplified: σ = excess ÷ Sharpe; β = excess ÷ Treynor; ρ = β × σ_m ÷ σ; R² = ρ².

cards.front: Jensen's alpha and Treynor given for a fund — how do you find β and R_f?

back.simplified: Expected (CAPM) return = actual − alpha. Write E = R_f + β × premium and Treynor = (actual − R_f) ÷ β; solve the two equations (Smart: β 0.35, R_f 6%).

cards.front: NAV ₹80 (95% equity), Sharpe 1.5, σ 10, Treynor 12, monthly cost ₹0.50, market +2%. NAV after a month?

back.trap: The paper printed Treynor 1.2; ICAI's answer used 12.

sections.title: Fund managers, FIIs and formula plans

cards.front: Fund manager's primary job in an active fund vs a passive fund?

back.simplified: Active: outperform the market and generate positive alpha through research and stock picking. Passive: match the index with minimum tracking error.

cards.front: Four other roles of a fund manager?

back.simplified: C-M-W-O: Compliances (SEBI/AMFI, reporting, documents); constant Monitoring of performance; Wealth creation and protection; control over Outsourced work.

cards.front: How do FIIs buy MF units, and what three benefits do they bring?

back.simplified: Directly from the issuer or through a registered broker on a recognised exchange, within SEBI limits. Benefits: better corporate governance, more competition, capital inflow (jobs and forex).

cards.front: Constant ratio plan: what do you do when the trigger is hit?

back.simplified: Total value = bonds + units × NAV; reset both halves to the fixed ratio — buy units after a fall, sell after a rise.
cases: SM TYK Sunidhi: ending ₹2,40,647.55 vs buy-and-hold ₹2,60,000
back.trap: ICAI checks each month's NAV against the previous month (32 → 38 = +18.75% triggers a sale).

cards.front: A fund holds ₹90 cr equity (β 1.1) and ₹10 cr cash. How many index futures (4,300 × 50) to hedge?

back.simplified: 1.1 × 90 crore ÷ (4,300 × 50) = 4,605 contracts. Cash is not hedged (MTP May 2025 S-II).

cards.front: When does a constant ratio plan beat buy-and-hold, and when does it lose?

back.simplified: It wins in a choppy market that ends near where it started (it keeps selling high, buying low). It loses in a strong one-way rise, because it keeps selling the winner (SM: ₹2,40,647.55 vs ₹2,60,000).

cards.front: Why is a SIP investor's average cost per unit lower than the average NAV?

back.simplified: A fixed amount buys more units when NAV is low, fewer when high — cost = total ₹ ÷ total units = harmonic mean of NAVs ≤ arithmetic mean.

cards.front: SIP vs STP vs SWP?

back.simplified: SIP: fixed amount in, regularly. SWP: fixed amount out, regularly. STP: fixed amount moved from one scheme (often liquid) to another (often equity).

cards.front: Jensen's alpha, M² and information ratio — one line each.

back.simplified: Alpha: return above CAPM for its β. M²: R_f + Sharpe × σ_m, compared with R_m. IR: (R_p − R_benchmark) ÷ tracking error.

cards.front: NFO, AUM, folio, cut-off time — what is each?

back.simplified: NFO: first subscription period. AUM: assets managed at market value. Folio: investor account number. Cut-off time: before it you get that day's NAV; after it, the next day's (no buying at a known NAV).

cards.front: ₹200 cr fund, 20 cr units, ₹10 cr bond defaults and is side-pocketed. Main NAV? Recovery of 40% is worth?

back.simplified: Main NAV = 190 ÷ 20 = ₹9.50. Recovery ₹4 cr ÷ 20 cr units = ₹0.20 per segregated unit, paid only to holders on the segregation date.

cards.front: How is the expense ratio actually charged?

back.simplified: 1/365 of the TER is deducted from net assets every day before NAV is struck: ₹500 cr × 1.5% ÷ 365 = ₹2.05 lakh a day.

practice.prompt: PYQ Nov 2024 · Q2(a) · 6 marks — Mr. X invested ₹1,00,000 at a face value of ₹10 per unit in a dividend reinvestment plan of a mutual fund during its initial public offering on 1st July, 2022. On 31st March, 2023 the fund declared a dividend of 10%, when Mr. X calculated his holding period return to be 115%. On 31st March, 2024 the fund declared a dividend of 20%; Mr. X redeemed all his investment and calculated his holding period return to be 193.134%. Calculate (i) the NAVs as on 31.03.2023 and 31.03.2024; (ii) the total units redeemed.
hints: HPR is already for the period — do not scale by months
NAV on the dividend date is ex-dividend: deduct the dividend from the value first
Dividend % is on face value ₹10

practice.prompt: PYQ May 2025 · Q5(a) · 7 marks — On 1st April, an open-ended scheme of Progressive Mutual Fund had 800 lakh units outstanding with NAV of ₹44.30 per unit. At the end of April, it issued 16 lakh units at opening NAV plus 2% load, adjusted for dividend equalization. At the end of May, 8 lakh units were repurchased at opening NAV less 2% exit load adjusted for dividend equalization. At the end of June, 60% of its available income was distributed as dividend. April–June quarter (₹ lakh): portfolio value appreciation 965.280; income of April 49.440; May 75.070; June 93.710. Calculate up to 4 decimals: (i) income available after distribution of dividend; (ii) issue price at the end of April; (iii) repurchase price at the end of May; (iv) NAV per unit as on 30th June.
hints: Income per unit each month = month's income ÷ units outstanding at that time
Issue price = NAV + load + income per unit to date
Closing NAV = opening net assets + appreciation + issue proceeds + income − repurchases − dividend
practice.modelAnswer:
(i) Income available
                                   Units   Per unit   ₹ lakh
Income from April                   800    0.0618    49.4400
Add: equalisation on issue           16    0.0618     0.9888
                                    816    0.0618    50.4288
Add: Income from May                       0.0920    75.0700
                                    816    0.1538   125.4988
Less: equalisation on repurchase      8    0.1538    (1.2304)
                                    808    0.1538   124.2684
Add: Income from June                      0.1160    93.7100
                                    808    0.2698   217.9784
Less: Dividend paid (60%)                  0.1619  (130.7870)
Income available                    808    0.1079    87.1914

(ii) Issue price = 44.3000 + 2% load 0.8860 + equalisation 0.0618 = ₹45.2478

(iii) Repurchase price = 44.3000 − 0.8860 + 0.1538 = ₹43.5678

(iv) Closing NAV (₹ lakh)
Opening net assets (44.30 × 800)      35,440.0000
Portfolio appreciation                   965.2800
Issue of units (16 × 45.2478)            723.9648
Income received                          218.2200
                                      37,347.4648
Less: Repurchase (8 × 43.5678)          (348.5424)
Less: Dividend                          (130.7870)
Closing net assets                    36,868.1354
Closing units                              808 lakh
NAV on 30 June                         ₹45.6289
markingPoints: Income per unit table with equalisation on issue and repurchase

practice.prompt: PYQ May 2023 · Q5(a) · 8 marks — M/s. Promising, an AMC, on 01.04.2018 floated a Dividend Reinvestment Plan and a Bonus Plan; Mr. X invested in both. Details (₹): 31.12.2019 bonus 1:5, NAV DRP 58 / BP 70; 31.03.2020 dividend 12%, NAV 60 / 72; 31.03.2021 dividend 10%, NAV 68 / 75; 31.03.2022 dividend 15%, NAV 75 / 66; 31.12.2022 bonus 1:3, NAV 70 / 60; 31.03.2023 NAV 80 / 71. Investment: DRP ₹10,80,000, BP ₹10,00,000. Average profit (DRP) ₹1,21,824; average yield (BP) 8.40%. Face value ₹10. Calculate the issue price of both schemes as on 01.04.2018.
hints: Total gain = average × 5 years
Undo each reinvestment: N + N × dividend ÷ NAV = units after
Undo bonuses latest first
markingPoints: Total value from average profit / yield over 5 years
Reinvested units removed with NAV ÷ (NAV + dividend)

practice.prompt: PYQ Dec 2021 · Q1(b) · 8 marks — Closed-ended equity schemes on 31/08/2021: AJ Mutual Fund NAV ₹80 (95% equity, rest cash), Sharpe 1.5, Treynor 12, σ 10; RP Mutual Fund NAV ₹61 (₹60 equity, rest cash), Sharpe 3, Treynor 10, σ 6. No change in portfolios during September. Monthly cost ₹0.50 per unit for each scheme. The share market rose by 2% in September. Calculate the expected NAV per unit on 30/09/2021 for both schemes.
hints: β = Sharpe × σ ÷ Treynor
Only equity moves with the market
Cash falls by the month's cost
practice.modelAnswer:
Working notes
(i) Equity and cash        AJ        RP
NAV                       80.00     61.00
Equity element            76.00     60.00
Cash element               4.00      1.00

(ii) Beta
AJ: Sharpe 1.5 = (E(R) − Rf) ÷ 10 → 15; Treynor 12 = 15 ÷ β → β = 1.25
RP: Sharpe 3 = (E(R) − Rf) ÷ 6 → 18; Treynor 10 = 18 ÷ β → β = 1.80

(iii) Equity rises: AJ 2% × 1.25 = 2.50%; RP 2% × 1.80 = 3.60%

(iv) Cash after a month: AJ 4.00 − 0.50 = 3.50; RP 1.00 − 0.50 = 0.50

Expected NAV on 30.09.2021
AJ: 76 × 1.025 = 77.90 + 3.50 = ₹81.40
RP: 60 × 1.036 = 62.16 + 0.50 = ₹62.66

(Note: the question paper printed AJ's Treynor as 1.2; ICAI's answer used 12.)
markingPoints: Split NAV into equity and cash

practice.prompt: PYQ Sep 2025 · Q3(b) · 4 marks — Mr. DK has 1,000 units of AM Mutual Fund. NAV is ₹17.50 at the beginning and ₹18.90 at the end of the year. Option I: pay ₹1.50 per unit as dividend and ₹1.20 per unit as capital gain. Option II: reinvest these distributions at an average NAV of ₹17.30 per unit. Compute the holding period return for both options and select the preferable option (2 decimals).
hints: Option I: (change in NAV + dividend + CG) ÷ opening NAV
Option II: extra units = distributions ÷ 17.30
practice.modelAnswer:
Option I (per unit)
Change in price 18.90 − 17.50 = 1.40
Dividend 1.50; capital gain 1.20
Total reward 4.10 ÷ 17.50 = 23.43%

Option II
Distribution = 1,000 × (1.50 + 1.20) = ₹2,700
Additional units = 2,700 ÷ 17.30 = 156.07
Total units = 1,156.07 × ₹18.90 = ₹21,849.72
Cost = 1,000 × 17.50 = ₹17,500
Return = (21,849.72 − 17,500) ÷ 17,500 = 24.86%

Conclusion: reinvestment (Option II) gives the higher holding period return and is preferable.
markingPoints: Option I total reward ₹4.10 per unit

practice.prompt: PYQ Jan 2026 · Q6(a) · 6 marks — Stork Capital launched its first NFO on June 1, 2024 at ₹10 per unit and received subscriptions for 180 lakh units. Griffin Securities underwrote the entire issue of 200 lakh units for 2.0% commission. Initial investments ₹1,780 lakh; marketing expenses ₹25 lakh. During FY ended March 31, 2025 it sold securities costing ₹250 lakh for ₹280 lakh and bought securities for ₹265 lakh. Management expenses cannot exceed 0.50% of average funds invested; actual ₹5.50 lakh, of which ₹0.50 lakh outstanding. Dividends earned ₹5.0 lakh, of which ₹0.40 lakh uncollected. It distributes 80% of all realised earnings. Market value of portfolio on March 31, 2025 ₹2,150.50 lakh. Determine the closing NAV per unit (2 decimals).
hints: Underwriter takes up the whole 200 lakh units
Chargeable expense = lower of actual and the cap
Uncollected dividend is a receivable
practice.modelAnswer:
(1) Opening cash (₹ lakh)
NFO proceeds 200 × 10 = 2,000.00
Less: initial investments (1,780.00), underwriting 2% (40.00), marketing (25.00)
Opening cash = 155.00

(2) Management expenses
Average funds = (1,780 + 1,795) ÷ 2 = 1,787.50; cap 0.50% = 8.94
Chargeable = lower of 5.50 and 8.94 = 5.50; paid = 5.00

(3) Closing cash
155.00 + 280.00 (sale) + 4.60 (dividend collected) − 265.00 (purchases) − 5.00 (expenses) − 24.00 (80% of ₹30 lakh gain) − 4.00 (80% of ₹5 lakh dividend) = 141.60

NAV
Cash 141.60 + portfolio 2,150.50 + dividend receivable 0.40 = 2,292.50
Less: outstanding expenses (0.50) = 2,292.00
Units 200 lakh → NAV ₹11.46

(ICAI also accepts distributing 80% of the ₹4.60 lakh collected: NAV still ₹11.46.)

practice.prompt: PYQ May 2023 · Q6(c) · 4 marks — Index Funds is one of the Special Funds. What are the other funds in the Special Funds category?
hints: Eight types in SM para 2.2.3 besides index funds
practice.modelAnswer:
(a) International funds — raise money in India, invest globally.
(b) Offshore funds — raise money globally, invest in India.
(c) Sector funds — whole fund in one industry (power, IT, pharma).
(d) Money market funds — debt-oriented; preservation of capital, liquidity and moderate income through CPs, CDs, T-bills, G-secs.
(e) Fund of funds — invest in units of other MF schemes of the same or other fund houses.
(f) Capital protection oriented funds — protection from portfolio structure (not a guarantee); close-ended, listed, rated.
(g) Gold funds — track gold, usually as ETFs listed on the exchange.
(h) Quant funds — data-driven, rule-based models decide stock, quantity and timing.

practice.prompt: MTP Nov 2024 S-I · Q2(c) · 4 marks — Explain the various qualitative factors that need to be taken into account, in addition to quantitative factors, to evaluate the performance of any mutual fund.
hints: Portfolio, fund manager, fund house
practice.modelAnswer:
(1) Quality of portfolio — blue-chip and large companies, diversification, style (growth, value, blend); for debt funds credit quality, average maturity and modified duration; investments must match the objective; a lower portfolio turnover ratio is generally better.
(2) Track record and competence of the fund manager — knowledge, ability to manage, past performance, conviction.
(3) Credibility of the fund house team — redemptions, crediting of dividends, adequate information to investors.
markingPoints: Quality of portfolio with equity and debt aspects
Fund manager's track record and competence

practice.prompt: RTP Nov 2026 · Q10 — A fund holds five Government bonds, face value ₹5 crore each: GOI 2026 (11.68%, price 106.50, duration 3.50), GOI 2030 (7.55%, 105.00, 6.50), GOI 2035 (7.38%, 105.00, 7.50), GOI 2042 (8.35%, 110.00, 8.75), GOI 2052 (7.95%, 101.00, 13.00). (i) Identify the type of fund. (ii) NAV per unit if units are 2.50 crore. (iii) Suggest churning to reduce risk if rates are expected to (A) fall 25 bp, (B) rise 75 bp, and compute the revised duration (simple average).
hints: Only dated Government securities
Value = ₹5 crore × price ÷ 100
Rates down → lengthen; rates up → shorten
practice.modelAnswer:
(i) Gilt fund — invested only in dated Government securities.

(ii) Investment (₹ lakh): 532.50 + 525.00 + 525.00 + 550.00 + 505.00 = 2,637.50
NAV = 2,637.50 ÷ 250 = ₹10.55

(iii) Average duration = 39.25 ÷ 5 = 7.85 years
(A) Rates fall: sell GOI 2026, buy GOI 2052 → (39.25 − 3.5 + 13) ÷ 5 = 9.75 years
(B) Rates rise: sell GOI 2052, buy GOI 2030 → (39.25 − 13 + 6.5) ÷ 5 = 6.55 years
(Buying GOI 2026 is not preferred: its maturity is very short and a 75 bp move is comparatively large.)
